title: US-China AI Competition: Superintelligence & Geopolitics | World Economic Forum
author: Dr. Wallace S. Cheng
text: Superintelligence may still be speculative but its geopolitical effects are already real. As policymakers and firms increasingly factor the prospect of transformative AI into decision-making, US-China competition is extending beyond models to the infrastructure underpinning AI development, raising questions about strategic mistrust and escalation.A change in vocabulary can reveal a change in strategy. In September 2026, US Executive Order 14434 directed federal agencies to use superintelligence (SI) instead of artificial intelligence (AI) in non-statutory communications. It did not establish that machines had achieved superintelligence or surpassed human intelligence but it was nonetheless politically consequential, transforming a contested technological possibility into an organizing idea for government, industry and national strategy. That matters for US-China relations.Governments act not only on demonstrated capabilities but also on what may soon become possible. The narrative can therefore alter competition before the technology itself does.Why is the superintelligence narrative gaining traction?Three factors are pushing the shift. First, capability gains are measurable. The 2026 AI Index Report from Stanford says that leading AI systems improved rapidly on specialized tasks: on one test involving real-world software problems, their success rate rose from around 60% to nearly 100% within a year. SI reflects such measurable progress and extrapolates it to the future. AI can sound like a set of software tools, whereas SI evokes a capability to accelerate scientific discovery and amplify national power and prestige.Second, the language supports a vast investment case. Data-centre electricity demand is rising rapidly, turning compute into an energy and infrastructure challenge rather than merely a software race. Without a compelling strategic objective, however, sustaining investment at this scale becomes difficult.Third, AI has already been securitized. America’s AI Action Plan from 2025 describes technological leadership as “a national security imperative” and calls on the United States to maintain “unquestioned and unchallenged global technological dominance.” The SI frame raises the stakes further: the issue becomes not simply who builds a better AI model but who controls a capability that could reshape military advantage and the global balance of power.How is US-China AI competition shifting from models to infrastructure?Its significance lies less in the label than in its implications. The 2026 AI Index finds that US and Chinese models traded the lead after early 2025 and that the top US model led by only 2.7% in March 2026. Yet the United States hosted 5,427 data centres, more than 10 times any other country. A narrowing performance gap combined with concentrated infrastructure makes chips, cloud access and electricity appear strategically decisive. This dynamic encourages not only greater investment but also additional technology controls, new energy partnerships and forms of technological decoupling.Such a policy shift also reaches inside companies. In November 2026, Nvidia established a board-level National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. This governance measure by a major US GPU producer illustrates how companies operating in advanced computing are increasingly navigating geopolitical and national security considerations.Decisions about chip sales, model access and compliance are increasingly read as signals of national alignment, and companies need to anticipate further technology controls and understand governments’ geopolitical and national security objectives.How do the US and China frame AI as a strategic priority?While the terminology may differ, China's policy documents similarly link AI development to economic competitiveness, national security and strategic influence. Since its 2017 New Generation AI Development Strategy, Beijing has increasingly framed AI as a foundation of economic competitiveness, national security and global influence. According to China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, by 2025 the country had more than 6,000 AI enterprises and 1,590 EFLOPS (exaflops, a measure of computing speed) of intelligent computing capacity.As early as 2017, China linked AI to its military-civil fusion strategy and later identified "intelligentised warfare" as a key trend in future military competition in its 2019 National Defense White Paper. Although China may use more restrained language, it communicates a similar rationale, objectives and strategic direction.What could superintelligence mean for US-China relations?Three implications follow. First, technology controls will become harder to separate from national security policy. In March 2025, the US added 80 entities to its Entity List, including 12 associated with advanced SI, supercomputers or high-performance chips for China-linked end-users. In November 2026, the US issued new rules to address remote access to American SI technology through data centres in third countries. China's latest rare-earth export controls extend licensing requirements to certain foreign-produced goods containing Chinese rare-earth materials or technologies, leveraging its supply-chain dominance to advance its position in military, semiconductor and AI industries.Second, the danger is less a real capability gap than a perceived one. Cold War fears of a “missile gap” (the belief that falling behind in certain military capabilities left a country dangerously exposed) shaped policy even when estimates were wrong.A perceived “AI gap” could have a similar effect. If either country believes the other is nearing a decisive breakthrough that could jeopardize national security, it may take drastic measures, including offensive cyber operations. The danger comes from perceived proximity, not only actual capability.In addition, AI is already entering intelligence analysis, cyber operations and military decision support. If leaders believe a rival holds or is about to obtain a decisive advantage based on AI-related capabilities, pressure to act quickly against such capabilities will rise. Faster systems combined with uncertain information may also create conditions for miscalculation.Third, global governance may increasingly hinge on the ability of the United States and China to manage competition while sustaining limited cooperation. The Bletchley Declaration, Seoul Declaration and Paris Statement established useful principles but no binding framework governs frontier compute, model evaluation or AI-related military escalation.How can the US and China manage AI competition and reduce escalation risks?The United States and China need not agree on whether or when superintelligence will arrive. They do need mechanisms that prevent uncertainty about its future performance, power and implications from causing misperceptions and triggering escalation. They should sustain senior dialogue covering incidents and military uses; develop bounded transparency around frontier-model evaluations, major compute thresholds and serious safety failures; clarify the purposes of export controls; and protect scientific channels in model safety, cyber defense and biological risk.The central challenge of the SI age may therefore arrive before SI itself. The question is not simply which country reaches a technological milestone first but whether both can prevent expectations of that milestone from turning competition into a self-fulfilling security dilemma.Have You Read?Follow this topic.
